title: Let Them Eat Cake? 15 Yrs Before Marie Antoinette's Birth｜Curio Archive
description:
Did Marie Antoinette really say "Let them eat cake"? The earliest page that puts the line in black and white describes a day 15 years before she was born.
For anyone who has heard the line and wants to know where it really came from.

This episode goes in order: a young tutor in Lyon around 1740 who did not dare walk into a bakery; two letters the queen wrote to her mother after the 1775 Flour War, mentioning how dear bread was; Book Six of Rousseau's Confessions, printed in 1782; the "they say" written by the writer Alphonse Karr in Les Guêpes (The Wasps) in 1841, and his own retraction two years later; and a countess's memoir, published in 1907, that names someone else.

The original word is brioche (a bread made with butter and eggs); the first English translation called it "pastry", and "cake" became the usual rendering only later. Some things the records cannot settle: the year Rousseau reached Book Six is uncertain, he himself said Part One was written from memory and full of errors, and some scholars suspect he invented the princess; we have not found the 1760 book Karr mentions; the countess's account is hearsay. Whether the queen ever said anything else at some other time, no record can answer. Where the video says "I think" or "we think", that is this channel's view; sources are listed below.

Information as of 2026-10-19

Illustrations in this episode are AI-generated.

t001.text: You know it: let them eat cake.

t002.text: They say Marie Antoinette said it.

t003.text: Still on her: a queen blind to her people's pain.

t005.text: And an older book with the line set it 15 years before she was born.

t006.text: Odd: writing to her mother, she did mention bread.

t007.text: Her earliest known recorder said 2 years on: likely not her.

t008.text: So did Marie Antoinette really say let them eat cake?

t009.text: In order, from a pastry shop.

t010.text: It begins in May 1740, in Lyon.

t011.text: A 27-year-old moves into a provost's home.

t014.text: A little Jura white wine; very good, he says.

t015.text: His rule: wine always with food.

t016.text: Just buy bread, right? He didn't dare.

t017.text: Armed, yet scared to buy bread?

t018.text: He wrote: a fine gentleman with a sword, buying bread? Unthinkable.

t019.text: You know it: too well dressed for a small shop.

t025.text: Told peasants had no bread: let them eat brioche.

t026.text: So, as a last resort: buy brioche.

t020.text: Even that was hard: he'd pass thirty pastry shops, not daring to enter.

t021.text: Alone, just for brioche, at times all over town.

t022.text: And only one person could be inside,

t023.text: and with a face he liked.

t027.text: Brioche: butter-and-egg bread, a luxury then.

t028.text: Note: bread, not cake. So where did cake come from? Soon.

t030.text: That shy tutor was Rousseau. He left Lyon after a year.

t031.text: That was around 1740; Marie Antoinette was born 15 years later.

t032.text: So how do we know such a small thing?

t033.text: 20-odd years on, he put it in a book.

t034.text: England, then a château: Part One.

t036.text: Book Six's pastry shops? Written there? Unsure.

t037.text: In it he says he's frail and nearly sixty.

t038.text: Think: how well can an old man recall his twenties?

t039.text: Note his verb: "I recalled." Not fresh news, but an old memory.

t040.text: He admitted: all memory, many errors.

t041.text: Some scholars think he made it up.

t042.text: What's sure: he knew the tale.

t043.text: And where was the future queen?

t044.text: Born in Vienna in 1755, she was still there, a young girl.

t045.text: When he wrote it, she wasn't yet 13 and hadn't seen France.

t046.text: April 1770: proxy wedding; May: Versailles, at 14.

t047.text: Four years later, in 1774, at 18, she became queen.

t048.text: Legend says she said it as the French lacked bread. Did that happen?

t049.text: Yes: the spring after she became queen, bread prices rose.

t050.text: Bread mattered: biographers estimate it took half of pay.

t051.text: Your biggest bill jumps. Would you protest?

t052.text: So a biographer called bread the nation's obsession.

t053.text: Spark: grain trade freed last fall.

t054.text: Then in April and May, riots hit the north, east and west;

t055.text: Early May: mobs at Versailles' gate.

t056.text: Next day, Paris bakeries were looted: dubbed the Flour War.

t057.text: Scholars say it hurt her name with the people.

t058.text: Worse: anti-royal pamphlets called her Madame Deficit,

t060.text: I think that's why the words stick to her: foreign, lavish, and queen.

t061.text: Did she know bread was dear?

t062.text: Yes, she wrote it. On June 11 that year, the King was crowned;

t063.text: June 22, 11 days on: a letter home.

t064.text: Her mother: Austria's Empress Maria Theresa; letters printed in the 1860s.

t065.text: She wrote: two months on, they still welcome us. Sadly, bread is still dear.

t066.text: "Suffering, yet so kind to us: we must work for their good."

t067.text: The King, she said, seemed to grasp it.

t069.text: No. Three weeks later: people suffered much from dear bread.

t072.text: At 19, she hardly sounds like an eat-cake type.

t073.text: So do they prove she didn't?

t074.text: No. They show her attitude, not her words.

t075.text: A letter home shows just that day's mood.

t076.text: Rousseau died in 1778, the book still unprinted.

t077.text: Four years later, in 1782, Geneva printed Part One of his Confessions.

t078.text: Lyon is in Book Six; a Lausanne edition that year has it too.

t080.text: He doesn't say: no name, country or year.

t081.text: By then, Marie Antoinette was 26, queen for eight years.

t082.text: This is neat: readers then had a queen right beside them.

t083.text: A year on, the first English version made brioche "pastry";

t084.text: Oddly, the same passage calls it "a little cake."

t086.text: But scholars say the line isn't in them.

t087.text: Odd: by this account, the era that hated her most lacks it.

t088.text: Writing pamphlets against her, would you skip that line?

t089.text: She died in 1793; no known text credits her yet.

t090.text: 48 years later, in November 1841, writer Alphonse Karr printed it.

t091.text: In Les Guêpes he wrote: they say Marie Antoinette once said,

t093.text: Note: they say, true or not. Karr passed it on, he didn't invent it.

t094.text: Karr wrote again 2 years on. Saying what?

t095.text: It was 1843. He recalled a rumor spread back then

t096.text: that, told "the people" had no bread, she said it; when, he doesn't say.

t097.text: He'd just chanced on a 1760 book, he said,

t098.text: pinning the same line on whom? A duchess of Tuscany.

t099.text: Karr wrote: this roughly proves she didn't say it,

t100.text: but found and used on her.

t101.text: See? Her earliest known recorder later said: probably not her.

t106.text: In 60 years on the road, it even changed listeners.

t107.text: The story isn't over. Does any record name the speaker?

t108.text: Aside: the 1903 English version still says pastry.

t109.text: In 1907, a countess's memoir came out.

t110.text: It names her: Louis XV's daughter, Madame Victoire.

t111.text: Her verdict: dim, but very kind.

t113.text: In a shortage, told the poor had no bread, Madame Victoire

t114.text: said in tears: "Oh God, if only they'd make do with pâté crust!"

t117.text: Here she isn't cold, but kind.

t119.text: The countess, born only in 1781, heard it secondhand.

t120.text: She began writing in 1835, in her fifties.

t121.text: Cake came later as the usual English wording.

t122.text: Rewind: a Lyon tutor scared of bakeries recalls a princess;

t123.text: 40-odd years on, his book; earliest known text naming her, nearly 60 years after.

t124.text: We think it seeks an owner: we need a princess blind to bread costs.
